items.titleOriginal: Kids built taller spaghetti towers than business school grads by doing something adults forgot how to do
items.description: Ο Tom Wujec έχει περάσει χρόνια ταξιδεύοντας σε όλο τον κόσμο με μια χούφτα ξυλάκια σπαγγέτι. Ως μέρος των εταιρικών του εργαστηρίων για τη δημιουργία ομάδας, συχνά ζητά από τις ομάδες να κάνουν μια ανόητη, ανόητη εργασία: να φτιάξουν έναν πύργο από στεγνά μακαρόνια και ταινία, να τον κάνουν όσο το δυνατόν πιο ψηλό και να τον χτίσουν αρκετά δυνατό ώστε να κρατήσει το βάρος ενός marshmallow. Α, και κάντε το γρήγορα.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Tom Wujec has spent years traveling the globe with a handful of spaghetti sticks. As part of his corporate team-building workshops, he often asks groups to do a silly, counterintuitive task: build a tower out of dry spaghetti and tape, make it as tall as possible, and build it strong enough to hold the weight of one marshmallow. Oh, and do it fast. “The Marshmallow Challenge is a fun and instructive design exercise that encourages teams to work in these conditions to learn profound lessons in collaboration, innovation, and creativity,” he says. “It’s simple, fun, and instructive.” But now, having done the exercise with groups of all ages and backgrounds around the world, he’s learned a lot about who succeeds at the challenge and who struggles. Kids routinely outperform business school grads in marshmallow challenge A surprising group repeatedly appears in Wujec’s data and observations as having difficulty with the Marshmallow Challenge : “On every measure… the group that consistently does the worst is recent graduates of business school. MBA students. They suck. They’re terrible,” he teases in a TED Talk. As for groups that do well? The usual suspects, of course: engineers and architects. But another group seems to shine wherever Wujec takes his bundle of supplies: kindergarteners and all manner of young school kids. Why kids are amazing at building fast Wujec says that many of the groups he studies, and especially the business students, waste a lot of time. They have 18 minutes to complete their tower, and many adults spend a good portion of that time debating ideas and jockeying for leadership within the group. Then, they spend far too long planning and strategizing. You might expect kids to be exceedingly creative and good at thinking outside the box, and that’s true. Wujec notes that groups of kids come up with wild, truly unique designs that adults can’t conceive. But the other thing kids do well is fail. They’re not afraid of their tower falling down. So what do they do? They build fast, running with the first good idea they come up with. If it doesn’t work, and the tower won’t hold the marshmallow? They simply start again, with plenty of time left on the clock to iterate or start over completely. “They start with the marshmallow. They generally don’t talk, they stick things in the marshmallow. The marshmallow falls over, and they fix it, and start over,” Wujec explains. So while the business school grads are deciding who’s the leader of the group and sketching out their vision, the kids are already on their third prototype. Kindergarteners don’t just outperform business school grads—they do better than the average of all the groups Wujec has tested, and regularly outperform some whip-smart folks like lawyers and CEOs. In a LinkedIn post, behavioral scientist Michael Rucker writes that adults often fear failure much more than children. When trying something new, kids can be scared for many reasons, but their approach not working is usually not one of them. They lead with curiosity and fun, and they see what happens. The Marshmallow Challenge is a wonderful reminder for adults: what would it look like to just go for it? No waiting for permission, no jockeying for authority, just grabbing the marshmallow and going to work, knowing that every time it falls down, you’re one step closer to the ultimate goal, whatever it may be. The post Kids built taller spaghetti towers than business school grads by doing something adults forgot how to do appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Έρευνα αποκαλύπτει 5 μεγάλους λόγους που οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι που δεν πίνουν κρατούν τη νηφαλιότητά τους μυστική από τους άλλους
items.titleOriginal: Survey reveals 5 big reasons most non-drinkers keep their sobriety a secret from others
items.description: Η ποπ κουλτούρα απεικονίζει την κατανάλωση αλκοόλ ως έναν πανταχού παρόν κανόνα στην αμερικανική ζωή. Αλλά ένας εκπληκτικός αριθμός Αμερικανών στην πραγματικότητα δεν πίνουν καθόλου. Σύμφωνα με την Gallup, μόνο το 54%…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pop culture portrays drinking alcohol as a ubiquitous norm in American life. In films and TV shows, friends “grab a beer” together, dates “meet up for drinks,” guests bring wine as a gift, and people celebrate any an every big life event with champagne. But a surprising number of Americans don’t actually drink at all. According to Gallup , only 54% of adults in the U.S. drink alcohol, even occasionally. That means close to half of Americans don’t drink at all. One reason that number may be surprising is that a lot of sober folks are tight-lipped about it. In fact, a Boca Recovery Center survey found that 58% of non-drinkers hide their sobriety from certain people in their lives and 13% keep it a secret from everyone. But why? Let’s dive into the reasons behind the data. "The share of Americans who say they drink alcohol remains at a record-low 54% for the second consecutive year, the lowest reading in Gallup’s trend dating back to 1939." (via @gallup ) https://t.co/wzmiLyl19l pic.twitter.com/z6DcUkzDLG — John Gramlich (@johngramlich) August 20, 2026 Why fewer people are drinking Gallup data shows that in 1978, 71% of Americans drank alcohol, the highest in the past eight decades. In 2026, drinking hit a record low of 54%. There are lots of reasons people choose sobriety. Some people don’t like the way alcohol makes them feel. Others stop drinking after developing an addiction to it. Some observe religious prohibitions on alcohol. Others don’t want the excess calories. Some might be taking a medication that is contraindicated with alcohol. Others just hate the taste. The health risks of alcohol have become a bigger consideration for many, according to Gallop. In 2016, only 26% of people believed that having one or two drinks per day was bad for your health. In 2026, nearly double that number—51%—say it’s unhealthy. And in the Boca Secret Sobriety Report, half of non-drinkers said they stopped drinking for their physical or mental health. Why do people hide their sobriety? Boca’s Secret Sober Report goes into the numbers of people who keep their sober status private from at least some people (58%), as well as the reasons people give for not revealing that they don’t drink. View this post on Instagram More than half keep it from their social media followers as well as from their manager or supervisor. More than a third keep it from people they’ve dated since quitting or from their coworkers. One in four don’t tell their friends and acquaintances they’re sober, and one in five don’t tell their family members. About 13% keep it secret from everyone. The most common reason for not telling people, which 65% of respondents indicated, is “It didn’t seem like a big deal.” After that, 19% said, “It’s too personal,” 15% wanted to avoid questions, 13% didn’t want to be labeled, and 13% didn’t want to be judged. How the numbers break down by generation Of the 13% of people who don’t tell anyone they’re sober, here’s the generational split: Gen X: 20% Millennials: 12% Baby boomers: 10% Gen Z: 5% Of the 50% of respondents who don’t drink for their mental or physical health: Gen X: 54% Millennials: 52% Baby boomers: 45% Gen Z: 44% Of the 25% of Americans who have tried an alcohol-free challenges, such as a 30-Day Break or Dry January: Millennials: 29% Gen Z: 26% Gen X: 23% Baby boomers: 10% Overall, even though they drink less than younger generations previously have, Gen Z still feels more pressure to drink than other generations do. In the Boca report, 69% of sober Gen Zers said they’ve been questioned, pressured, or teased about not drinking, compared to 49% of other sober Americans. Tips for navigating the social drinking vs. sobriety landscape There appears to be a glaring contradiction in some of the data, which may boil down to perception. The vast majority of respondents—a whopping 94%—said that a person doesn’t owe anyone an explanation for why they’re not drinking. Additionally, 93% of people said they wouldn’t think less of a coworker who doesn’t drink at an event. However, 52% of sober Americans say they’ve been questioned, pressured, or teased about not drinking. And 30% said they’ve disguised not drinking to blend in, such as giving a fake reason for not drinking or ordering a drink they didn’t intend to consume. So most people express that they’re okay with people not drinking, but that’s not always how it feels on the sober side of things. Boca offers these tips for protecting your sobriety when you know you’re going to be at an event where people are drinking: Keep a short answer ready: A simple, honest line like “I’m not drinking tonight” is usually enough, and it saves you from inventing a reason on the spot. Choose your own drink early: Ordering a soda, mocktail, or sparkling water as soon as you arrive can head off offers before they start. Tell one trusted person: Sharing your decision with a friend or coworker you trust gives you an ally who can help redirect the conversation. Give yourself permission to leave: If an event starts to feel like too much pressure, it’s okay to step outside or head home early. And for those who do drink and don’t want sober folks to feel pressured or judged: Avoid teasing people about not drinking (even good-natured teasing can be uncomfortable), offer non-alcoholic options as a legitimate choice and not a lesser alternative, and don’t dwell on the person’s choice not to drink. Treat it as the no big deal that it is. No one should feel like they need to hide being sober to fit in or avoid scrutiny. We can all let each other have our individual choices and preferences without judging anyone either direction. You can find the full Secret Sober Report from Boca Recovery Center here. The post Survey reveals 5 big reasons most non-drinkers keep their sobriety a secret from others appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένα τεστ καρδιάς σε δύο λεπτά: Πώς οι ιδρυτές του Dehradun κατασκεύασαν μια συσκευή ΗΚΓ σε μέγεθος τσέπης
items.titleOriginal: A Heart Test in Two Minutes: How Dehradun Founders Built a Pocket-Sized ECG Device
items.description: Για κάποιον που βιώνει πόνο στο στήθος ή δύσπνοια σε ένα απομακρυσμένο χωριό, η λήψη ΗΚΓ μπορεί να σημαίνει ότι θα ταξιδέψει αρκετά χιλιόμετρα στο πλησιέστερο νοσοκομείο. Μέχρι να γίνει η δοκιμή, πολύτιμα λεπτά μπορεί να έχουν ήδη χαθεί. Αυτό το κενό ήταν που οδήγησε τον Rajat Jain και τους συνιδρυτές του να δημιουργήσουν τη Sunfox Technologies, μια εταιρεία τεχνολογίας υγείας στο Dehradun,…
items.descriptionOriginal: For someone experiencing chest pain or breathlessness in a remote village, getting an ECG can mean travelling several kilometres to the nearest hospital. By the time the test is done, precious minutes may already have been lost. It was this gap that led Rajat Jain and his co-founders to build Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech company in Dehradun, Uttarakhand. They launched Spandan, a pocket-sized ECG device that connects to a smartphone. The device can record a medical-grade ECG and generate a report within minutes, without needing a conventional ECG machine, an external battery or an internet connection. Today, more than 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, reaching over 20,000 villages across 28 states. The technology has been used to screen around five million patients, and over 2,00,000 lives have been saved. The journey to making cardiac testing more accessible, however, began with a personal tragedy that changed the course of Rajat's life. The personal loss that started it For Rajat, the idea for Sunfox began with a loss that was difficult to make sense of. At 21, he lost a close friend to a heart attack. The experience made him realise that cardiac emergencies can strike without warning and that, even when help is available, the first few minutes can make a crucial difference. At the time, Rajat was a mechanical engineer working in the automotive field. But the loss made him look towards a problem that felt far more urgent: "How could technology make basic cardiac diagnosis available when a hospital or specialist was not close by?" Bill Gates listening to Rajat Jain demonstrate Spandan's prowess at ICMR HQ in Delhi. Spandan was selected among India's best healthcare innovations supported by ICMR. That question led him and his co-founders — Arpit Jain, Saurabh Badola, Nitin Chandola and Sabit Rawat — to start Sunfox Technologies in Dehradun in 2016. They began working on ways to make an ECG, one of the first tests doctors use when a patient shows signs of a heart problem, smaller, more affordable and easier to use. The prototype was developed in 2017, laying the groundwork for the company's effort to take cardiac screening into places where access to specialised care is limited. How a smartphone became an ECG machine An ECG, or electrocardiogram, records the tiny electrical signals the heart produces with every beat. Doctors use it to identify a heart attack, a blocked artery or an irregular heartbeat. Traditionally, it requires a large machine, a trained technician and a hospital room. Spandan changes that. It is a portable 12-lead ECG device that connects to a smartphone, records the heart's signals and produces a report in about two minutes. "The advantage of using Spandan is that anyone with or without medical education can use it," says Jain. "Spandan devices use ECG sensors, smartphone integration, and software to record and display ECGs. It uses AI and analytics for report generation," he explains. "Also, it does not need an external battery to work; it uses power from your smartphone to work." That design was a deliberate choice, made with rural India in mind. "These features were very important for us as the device had to work in remote locations in the country without a regular source of electricity or internet connection," says Rajat. While the devices range in price from Rs 6,900 to Rs 75,000, depending on the model, Sunfox says a significant share of its users come from smaller towns and rural areas. Around 60 per cent of its users are from rural or semi-urban locations, with more than 20,000 devices currently active in these regions. Co-founders of Sunfox Technologies. Small clinics are among the buyers, as they see value in the device even at the Rs 16,000–17,000 price point, says the company. For healthcare facilities with limited access to conventional ECG machines, a portable device that can generate reports within minutes offers another way to conduct cardiac screening. For Sunfox, the goal was to make a heart test as routine as other everyday health checks, without hurting the wallet. Making cardiac monitoring accessible at home The device is also being used by individuals who want to monitor their heart health between doctor visits. Sandip Deodhar, 52, an accountant assistant from Kolhapur, has been using Spandan for the past month. He is hypertensive and diabetic, and says he would often spend Rs 200–300 every other week on ECG tests recommended during his consultations. After discovering Spandan online, he discussed it with his doctor, who agreed that he could use the device to record ECGs at home. "For the first three-four days, I ran multiple tests to review the reports and become accustomed to the device. Now, he tells me to notify him only if there is an abnormal test; otherwise, he says there's no need to even show him the report," says Sandip. The pilot: Testing in a hospital Before Spandan could go to villages, it had to prove itself inside a hospital. "We did the pilot in Fortis Hospital in Uttarakhand in 2018-19 along with SELCO Foundation," shares Rajat. The team wanted answers to two questions. "We were trying to prove the validity and accuracy of our devices and wanted to know how user-friendly our devices are so that frontline health workers with minimal trainin g could operate them." Then, in 2021, a study was conducted at Fortis Escorts Hospital in Dehradun under the supervision of cardiologists. The patients were first tested on the hospital's standard ECG machine. Within five minutes, the same patients were tested on Spandan, and a cardiologist reviewed the readings independently. Of the 153 patients enrolled, 110 were counted in the final results, and Spandan's reading matched that of the standard machine in 108 of those 110 cases. It was a small study, but it provided a base for what followed. Larger hospital studies came next, including a study of 2,799 patients, published in 2025 in the Anatolian Journal of Cardiology , and one in Meerut involving 184 patients with chest pain. The company says the count is now 30 studies. "We have compared the performance of Spandan with standard ECG devices in more than 30,000 patients and have achieved a 99.7% accuracy," says Rajat. How Sunfox found its footing Proving Spandan in a hospital was one step. Getting it into the field brought a different set of challenges. The first problem was money. "The biggest challenge for us was overcoming a funding crunch while developing a health device, which conventionally requires a large investment," says Rajat. In the early days, the founders paid for the work themselves. "When we first started, there was no funding or grant. We self-sponsored in most part and also did side-gigs to support the research and development of our devices," he recalls. The second problem was testing the device where it was meant to be used. A hospital in Dehradun is very different from a village clinic, and a device built for villages had to be tried in villages. "Secondly, we had difficulty in validating the results of our device in low-resource and rural areas because we couldn't get too many patients there," says Jain. There was also the matter of trust. Sunfox was entering India's medical device sector, which is known for high entry barriers, strict rules, heavy investment and a market crowded with imported products. Rajat says, "We faced constant doubts about whether medical technology built in India could be trusted." Help arrived in stages. In 2017, the first prototype was ready, and the team moved into its first office at a technology incubator at Graphic Era University in Dehradun. Government funding followed. "Later, we received funding from the state government of Uttarakhand, from our university, and also from the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, to conduct the pilot tests," says Jain. Private money came next. "In 2022, Sunfox appeared on Shark Tank India, where we got funding of Rs 1 crore," adds Rajat. Larger funding has followed since. In August 2024, Sunfox raised Rs 15 crore in a round led by Venture Catalysts. Inc42 also reports that the company had earlier received Rs 5 crore from USAID through its SAMRIDH Health programme and LetsVenture. Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In September 2026, Sunfox raised $7 million (INR 66 crore) in a Series A funding round led by renowned investor Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital and 3one4 Capital. The real-life challenge Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In December 2020, the Government of India's biotech agency BIRAC and the industry body Nasscom launched JanCare, a challenge offering health-tech startups pilot test beds at rural health centres in partnership with state governments. Sunfox took part, deploying eight devices across six CHCs and PHCs in Nagaland and two CHCs in Uttar Pradesh. In July 2022, Sunfox also worked with the Uttarakhand government to set up a free screening camp at Sonprayag, where the Kedarnath trek begins. Trained local volunteers screened pilgrims with Spandan and sent abnormal readings over WhatsApp to a cardiologist in Dehradun. In the first month, the camp screened nearly 1,500 people and referred 59 to a local doctor. These pilots showed that health workers without specialist training could operate the device, and larger deployments followed. SAMRIDH, the USAID-backed programme, says its support helped place 1,551 Spandan units in public and private clinics across Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Delhi, screening 63,486 people. From a prototype to 60,000 devices What began as a self-funded lab in Dehradun has since grown into a nationwide deployment. More than 60,000 Spandan devices are now in use, covering over 20,000 villages. "We have deployed over 60,000 devices in the country, from Himalayan states like Uttarakhand to Nagaland in the North-east and heavily forested and remote areas in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand," says Rajat. State governments have come on board. "We are working with the state governments of Uttarakhand and Haryana so that any patient with symptoms of heart ailments can get access to quick diagnosis and treatment," he says. The two-minute turnaround is particularly significant in these settings. "The healthcare worker, whether a nurse, technician or even doctor, puts the leads on the patient and receives an ECG within 3 minutes, with a clinician-reviewed diagnosis and prescription," Jain explains. The results show up in the numbers. Until October 2026, "In Uttarakhand, we have worked in CHCs and PHCs on the Char Dham Yatra route and have screened more than 13100 pilgrims and identified 463 critical patients who could receive treatment on time," he says. In Haryana, "We have deployed our devices in more than 597 PHCs and CHCs and conducted ECGs for 60,000 people and detected 2000 critical cases since June." The device can also flag the most dangerous kind of heart attack early. "We can detect the deadliest kind of heart attack, called STEMI, in less than an hour of it first occurring, saving thousands of lives," says Jain. The road ahead In August 2026, Sunfox marked 10 years with the opening of an innovation hub in Dehradun. Its next goal is to take Spandan beyond India. "We plan to expand in low- and middle-income countries, especially in Africa and South Asia, and we have already started." According to SAMRIDH, more than 400 Spandan devices are in use across Africa. The mission has not changed since the day Jain lost his friend. "Most heart attacks in India are preventable if diagnosed early," he says. "Our vision is to take this portable ECG technology and make it so ubiquitous that everyone has access to it, just as they do for thermometers and BP machines." And if the numbers are anything to go by, Sunfox is surely on its way to success.

items.title: Ο Billy Corgan σοκάρει το αστέρι του «Breakfast Club» εξηγώντας γιατί η ταινία αποτυπώνει τέλεια τον πόνο Gen X
items.titleOriginal: Billy Corgan shocks ‘Breakfast Club’ star by explaining why the film perfectly captures Gen X pain
items.description: Σε ένα πρόσφατο επεισόδιο του podcast The Magnificent Others, ο οικοδεσπότης της σειράς και frontman των Smashing Pumpkins, Billy Corgan, προσπάθησε να μοιραστεί μια νέα άποψη για το The Breakfast Club που ο καλεσμένος του, ο ηθοποιός Anthony Michael Hall, δεν είχε ξανακούσει. Ο Hall παραδέχτηκε ότι δεν μπορεί να μείνει μια μέρα χωρίς να μιλήσει για το κλασικό Gen X, οπότε ο Corgan έκοψε τη δουλειά του…
items.descriptionOriginal: On a recent episode of The Magnificent Others podcast, the show’s host and Smashing Pumpkins frontman, Billy Corgan, attempted to share a fresh perspective on The Breakfast Club that his guest, actor Anthony Michael Hall, had never heard before. Hall admitted he can’t go a day without talking about the Gen X classic , so Corgan had his work cut out for him. In the 1985 John Hughes classic, Hall played Brian Johnson, known as “The Brain.” “A lot of us were the latchkey kids. And the joke I always make is we were abandoned by our parents because of [deleted] and yoga,” Corgan joked. “So the reason I think that movie resonated so deeply? It’s kind of this bullying thing. I see that as a subplot. I think the key is all these kids have been abandoned by the people they should be relying on.” Why is ‘The Breakfast Club’ so important to Gen Xers? “I go to the most obvious point, the dynamics between the characters, let’s call it the kineticism between the characters. But the thing that started to strike me was, wait, they’re all in detention for a reason. And so, the subtext in my mind is they’ve been abandoned by something or somebody,” Corgan continued. Corgan taps into the idea that Gen Xers (1965 to 1980) are often called the least parented generation because they grew up when divorce was at an all-time high, more women were in the workplace , and children were allowed to roam free. In some ways, Gen Xers had incredible freedom that today’s kids should envy. In other ways, growing up as a latchkey kid or with parents who weren’t around was tantamount to neglect. Hall agreed with Corgans’ take. “You’re right. The loss that they all feel may be from their parents and what they’re not doing,” he responded. In the film, Allison Reynolds, the “Basket Case,” is clearly neglected by her parents. She tells Emilio Estevez’s character, “They ignore me.” Her strange behavior throughout the film feels like an attempt to be seen. The characters in ‘The Breakfast Club’ are all dealing with some form of neglect “When I think back on the film, I think it’s most clearly seen in Ally Sheedy’s character [“The Basket Case”]. That sense of neglect from her parents,” Hall added. “So, that’s a key word, and you brought up something really powerful here, which is what the parents weren’t doing that led them there.” The rest of the main characters in The Breakfast Club weren’t necessarily neglected in the sense that they weren’t given any attention, but they all lack a real emotional connection to their parents, which is just as painful. John “The Criminal” Bender is verbally and physically abused by his father, leading him to be rebellious. Claire “The Princess” Standish is used as a weapon in her parents’ marriage woes, making her feel like a pawn. Andrew “The Athlete” Clark’s parents push him too hard to win and be tough; he becomes a bully to overcompensate. Brian “The Brain” Johnson, Hall’s character, is so concerned with his grades that a bad mark makes him consider self-harm. In the end, the five teenagers from different social classes and cliques learn to lean on each other to get through detention and tell the principal that they are beyond categorization. Corgan believes this type of camaraderie mirrors the attitudes of kids in the alternative rock scene of the ’80s and ’90s that gave birth to the Smashing Pumpkins. “But at the end of the day, the reason I think it hits so hard is almost everybody in our generation was thinking ‘that’s me’ in that same dynamic, having to reach for people,” Corgan said. “One of the core ethos of alternative rock was we found community with a bunch of other weirdos because many of us were the land of lost toys. Who were we going to turn to?” The post Billy Corgan shocks ‘Breakfast Club’ star by explaining why the film perfectly captures Gen X pain appeared first on Upworthy .

Η 27χρονη πρόσφατα ολοκλήρωσε και τις 16 στάσεις στη γραμμή Victoria Line σε έναν μαραθώνιο σκίτσο 10 ωρών, ξεκινώντας με το Brixton και ολοκληρώνοντας με το Walthamstow Central. Πέρασε περίπου μισή ώρα σε κάθε στάση δ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve noticed more spiders lately, near window frames, behind boxes in the garage, lurking in basement corners, you’re not imagining it. Fall is mating season for spiders , which makes them more active than usual, and when temperatures drop, many of them make the same call you would and head inside. Of the roughly 3,700 spider species in the United States, only about 0.3 percent are dangerous to humans. The rest are, in the words of Oregon State University Extension horticulturist Brooke Edmunds , “minding their own business.” Two things converging in the spiderverse It’s not only the cold driving these arachnids indoors. Spiders like cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders move indoors as temperatures fall, and once inside, many are also looking for mates and somewhere quiet to leave their eggs . “Just like us, they’re coming inside to get warm,” Edmunds explains. “They aren’t aggressive toward people, not even the spiders.” Some females carry egg sacs on their bodies; others are hunting for corners, furniture undersides, the back of a closet, anywhere spider silk can hold a sac in place. That’s part of why fall can feel like a sudden invasion when it’s really just two instincts running in parallel. What makes your home The Destination Some of it is biology, and some of it is a gap in the garage door seal. If the weather strip at the bottom is worn or the door doesn’t sit flush, that’s an open invitation. Same goes for cracks along the foundation and gaps around window frames. And if your house already has gnats, flies, aphids, or termites, spiders will follow, because those critters happen to make up a great menu for our eight-legged friends. Outside, what’s close to the house does a lot of the inviting. Colorado State University’s entomology experts recommend clearing away rock piles, wood stacks, old boards, and compost heaps from around the perimeter. Spiders go for dark, damp, undisturbed spots. Tree limbs that touch or hang near windows are another way in, and crawl spaces packed with boxes are definitely attractive to them. How to keep them out Caulking cracks in your foundation and making sure screens and door seals are intact does a lot. Fall is also a good time to go through basements, garages, and closets, not for tidiness, but because those neglected corners are exactly what spiders are looking for. If you’re digging into old cardboard boxes or boots that haven’t moved since last winter, wear gloves. Spiders have sometimes made a cozy home inside them. If you’d rather not evict the ones already there, that’s fine too. They’re eating the insects you’d otherwise be swatting at, and most will move on once the season turns anyway. items.descriptionOriginal: We like to think we always know the right thing to do. Some lessons, however, come the hard way . We learn through mistakes and missteps, stumbling into victories through trial and error. Some lessons, it seems, we have to learn on our own, no matter what other people have tried to tell us. There are also hard truths that come from quiet reflection or mulling over guidance passed down from a mentor . Now add random internet comment sections to that list. A popular Reddit thread recently asked users to share the one piece of advice that permanently altered their perspective. The responses offer a powerful reminder to listen closely to others’ wisdom. Here are 10 life-changing pieces of advice that might just reshape your own journey. 1. Ask which choice lets you be who you really are. “When I consider options, I ask which choice lets me become more of myself? It doesn’t mean ‘always choose whatever feels good.’ Sometimes becoming more yourself requires doing something difficult, disciplined, or terrifying.” We often make decisions based on comfort or fear. This may seem like the easier route, but is it more beneficial for you in the long run? Asking which path brings you closer to your true self shifts the focus completely. Growth rarely happens inside our comfort zones. 2. Never pass up an opportunity to use the restroom. ” It has NEVER failed me to be proactive.” Anyone who has ever been stuck in gridlock traffic knows the profound truth of this rule. Urgency doesn’t always lead to the best options. Proactive comfort is an underrated life hack. 3. Be forgiving; it sure helps. A quote often misattributed to various speakers (Buddha, Saint Augustine, Nelson Mandela, etc.) goes: “Holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die.” Whoever said it, the message is clear: forgiveness is as much for you as it is for the other person. No one is saying you have to forget, either. This is about freeing yourself from another person’s emotional baggage. 4. Accentuate the positive. “If you’ve spent years conditioning yourself to think negatively about yourself, you can condition yourself in the other direction too. It might feel cheesy at first but keep reinforcing the positive until that starts becoming your default mindset. Just embrace the cheesiness for now and do it anyway.” Neural pathways take time to rewire. Your brain believes what you tell it every day. Embracing a little cheesiness is a small price to pay to push yourself toward a more positive path. 5. Stop expecting everyone else to act like you. “Not everyone thinks like I do – and that’s ok.” This one hits deep. We often get hurt when people don’t react, work, or care the way we do. The spark of your passion does not have to be lit by others. Realizing that everyone operates from their own blueprint can save you lots of heartbreak. 6. It’s an expense, not a problem. “A problem that can be solved with money isn’t a problem; it’s an expense.” Perspective changes everything when life throws a curveball. A flat tire or a broken appliance can feel devastating in the moment, so don’t add fuel to the fire. Remembering that it is a financial hurdle, not a life-or-death situation, helps keep stress in check. 7. Nobody will thank you for living up to their expectations. “Stop people-pleasing.” No one wants to be someone else’s source of stress, but people-pleasing is a quiet trap. At the end of the day, you are the one who has to live with your choices. Live a life that makes sense to you. 8. How much time did you spend thinking about other people’s mistakes today? “It wasn’t much, right? I stopped caring so much about what others think of me at that moment. I started making more decisions without regrets.” We spend so much energy worrying about how others judge us. In reality, most people are too focused on themselves to worry about you most of the time. Recognizing this truth brings instant freedom. 9. Say no to some things so you can say yes to others. “Totally changed my POV. That was thirty years ago, and it has informed my successful career.” Understanding your limits is important, especially in business. Every single “yes” you give away is a hidden “no” to your own time and priorities. Protecting your energy ensures you have enough left for what truly matters, both at work and at home. 10. Empathy with boundaries is compassion. Empathy without boundaries is self-destruction. “Needed to hear this right now. Thank you.” There are plenty of things in this world that spark concern and worry. Compassion is what connects us , building bridges of understanding and community. But you cannot pour from an empty cup. Caring deeply for others should never require you to sacrifice your own mental health or safety. Give, but give what you can afford. The post People share 10 ‘random pieces of advice’ that legitimately changed their lives appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? Reading Time: 5 minutes How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? When you envision a typical construction site, you likely picture roaring diesel engines, towering waste bins and clouds of dust. However, forward-thinking builders are proving that heavy-duty work doesn’t have to create heavy pollution. While traditional operations take a massive toll on the planet through emissions and discarded scrap, you can drive real change on the ground. By embracing thoughtful equipment care, cleaner energy and circular material sourcing, your crews can build a greener world from the ground up. 1. Prioritizing Low-Emissions and Salvaged Materials Every major construction project begins with a blueprint, but the materials you specify in those early drawings dictate your build’s lifetime environmental footprint. Traditional supplies like standard Portland cement and virgin structural steel carry staggering amounts of embodied carbon—the hidden greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, manufacturing, and transport. Many firms are swapping out carbon-intensive staples for lower-impact alternatives that still perform reliably. Mass timber, sustainably harvested from certified forests, sequesters atmospheric carbon right inside a building’s frame. Meanwhile, opting for supplementary materials, such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag — a recycled industrial by-product that can replace part of the cement in concrete — can significantly undercut the carbon emissions of traditional concrete mixes. Sustainability also means keeping things local and circular. By sourcing reclaimed lumber, crushed stone and recycled structural steel from regional deconstruction projects, you eliminate the fuel burned shipping heavy freight across the country. Salvaging high-quality elements prevents unnecessary virgin extraction, reduces procurement costs and gives historic materials a useful second life. 2. Adopting Proactive Machinery Maintenance to Reduce Waste and Boost Efficiency A truly sustainable jobsite isn’t just about what’s being built, but also about how efficiently machines run while building it. Proactive heavy equipment care is an essential pillar of low-impact construction. When diesel-powered machinery operates at peak mechanical efficiency, engines encounter less drag, burn significantly less fuel and prevent harmful oil leaks from threatening surrounding soil and local waterways. Routine inspections and precision adjustments prevent premature component breakdowns, keeping bulky metal and synthetic assemblies out of scrap heaps. Daily cleanings with a pressure washer clear away packed dirt and rocks that strain the undercarriage rollers, while maintaining proper track sag prevents engine strain and reduces excess fuel consumption. For example, checking the rubber tracks on skid steers to avoid wear and tear while encouraging optimal performance through proper tension reduces engine strain from overly tight tracks. Doing so means saving fuel and protecting components, leading to fewer emissions and a longer lifespan, which reduces manufacturing footprints. Prioritizing consistent preventive maintenance across excavators and loaders also curbs project delays and saves expenses. 3. Cutting Site Waste Through Circular Construction Practices Traditional construction projects generate mountains of debris, but progressive firms are more often viewing discarded materials as valuable future commodities. Moving toward a circular model begins with systematic on-site sorting, so instead of commingling off-cuts and packaging into generic roll-off dumpster bins, crews establish clearly labeled recovery stations for clean timber, scrap metal, cardboard and masonry. Processing materials directly where the work occurs can save significant hauling fuel and slash disposal tipping fees. Contractors often deploy portable rock crushers to break down clean demo concrete and masonry rubble on-site, producing quality sub-base aggregate to use for access roads, staging areas and sturdy foundation pads. When structures must come down, intentional deconstruction is replacing wrecking balls. Instead of demolishing older framing, crews carefully deconstruct timber and fixtures for repurposing in community projects or donation. Through active partnerships with local salvage yards and regional architectural reclaimers, firms keep large volumes of solid waste out of municipal landfills and help nearby communities access sturdy, character-rich, reusable materials. 4. Cleaning Up Fleet Power Heavy diesel machinery is a core part of commercial construction, but powering an entire fleet on fossil fuels carries a steep environmental and human price tag. Construction vehicles can emit substantial particulate matter and greenhouse gases, worsening local air quality while driving up fuel costs. Consequently, modern contractors are investigating ways to make fleet operations cleaner, quieter and more efficient. Electrification is leading this charge, especially among compact utility machinery. Battery-powered mini-excavators, electric wheel loaders and cordless hand tools deliver instant torque without generating smelly exhaust fumes or extreme noise levels. The shift to electric dramatically improves jobsite air quality, safeguards the respiratory health of on-site crews and earns goodwill from neighboring residential communities. Many larger diesel rigs cannot yet fully transition to electric powertrains, so operational discipline must bridge the sustainability gap. Establishing an automatic five-minute engine shut-off rule for loaders and haul trucks will reduce the exhaust fumes in the air while shaving gallons off daily diesel usage. Routine fuel tracking can ensure every engine runs at peak efficiency. 5. Leveraging Smart Planning and Modular Prefabrication Careful planning can make modern jobsites more efficient, with organized factory processes replacing crowded material storage areas. Modular prefabrication shifts significant building processes off-site into climate-controlled manufacturing facilities. In these organized plant environments, automated cutting systems reduce raw material scrap while optimizing usage down to the millimeter. Assembling wall panels off-site allows workers to recycle off-cuts and minimize on-site construction noise and dust. Simultaneously, modular construction eases neighborhood strain by slashing repetitive truck traffic. Instead of individual supply trucks trickling through local residential streets each day, preassembled building modules arrive in consolidated shipments. Digital project management platforms take this operational efficiency even further with advanced scheduling software accurately tracking incoming deliveries to ensure high-value lumber, drywall and delicate insulation arrive exactly when crews are ready to install them. As a result, there are fewer chaotic staging yards and likely a large reduction in expensive, weather-related material damage from heavy rain or exposure to damp ground. 6. Building a Jobsite Culture Around Everyday Sustainability Advanced equipment and green certifications certainly help, but authentic sustainability ultimately begins with people. Creating an eco-conscious jobsite means fostering a crew culture with daily habits that make resource conservation feel simple and worthwhile. The small decisions made throughout an ordinary shift quickly multiply across multi-month commercial developments. Simple operational swaps, like eliminating disposable water bottles in favor of refillable hydration stations and ditching single-use plastic wrap, drastically curb daily jobsite litter and establish an environmental mindset on the ground. Switching to energy-efficient LED lightbulbs in temporary site offices and encouraging shared crew transit foster an office and field culture in which eco-friendly choices become second nature. Sustainability-minded firms actively show their teams how these practical habits mirror broader everyday eco-friendly lifestyles. Incorporating simple sustainable living ideas into workers’ routines inspires tradespeople to make mindful, low-waste choices at home and at work. When crew members see company leadership genuinely backing these principles, green building becomes a shared source of pride instead of just a compliance task. Lay the Groundwork for a Cleaner Industry You can transform your construction operation into a more sustainable operation without overhauling everything overnight. True sustainability is an ongoing journey built on practical, everyday choices. By making each project cleaner, less wasteful and more efficient, you will make a tangible difference with every build. You hold the power to reshape the building landscape, proving that with each structure, you can construct a stronger, cleaner and more resilient tomorrow. The post How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India. In 2026, she retired after 42 years of service, leaving behind a legacy of compassion and dedication. One bicycle. One nurse. 42 years of service. items.descriptionOriginal: Chotu, 40, runs a pakori thela (fritters stall) outside the temple at Lalbagh in Moradabad. He has watched people's relationship with the nearby riverbank change. "Earlier, people watched the volunteers clean ; today, local people themselves feel responsible for keeping the ghat and river clean," he says. For Kapil Kumar, 35, who leads the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign, this willingness to take responsibility matters deeply. His team at Parivartan "The Change" reports completing more than 218 clean-up drives and removing over 1.2 lakh kg of waste, with more than 5,000 volunteers participating over the years. Behind those figures are conversations with visitors, residents making space for equipment, and volunteers returning to a riverbank they have come to care about. Getting here took several attempts. A teacher's question took him beyond his textbooks Kapil completed his B.Tech in mechanical engineering in 2013 and spent a year in the automobile sector. From 2014 to 2016, he pursued a PGDM while preparing for government examinations, including the UPSC Civil Services Examination. His UPSC preparation continued until 2017. Kapil and his friends founded Parivartan in October 2016 and registered it in July 2017. "During my UPSC preparation, studying sociology helped me look beyond individual issues and understand society, communities and the factors that influence social change. It gave me a much broader perspective on the challenges people face," he tells The Better India . In 2016, blogs he wrote to practise essays and answers drew responses from juniors and former college colleagues. "They asked me, 'Why don't we do something on the ground?' And that's where it all began. We started with a few activities and gradually built from there," he recalls. A visit to a government school in Moradabad gave that suggestion a practical meaning. Kapil found leaking roofs, inadequate washrooms and children without proper chairs and benches. When he questioned the conditions, a teacher challenged him. "People usually come here for surveys and other work, criticise the government and the administration, and then leave. But what can you actually do beyond criticism?" he recalls her asking. She pointed him towards a child with an eye problem. "So she asked me, 'Can you take him to the hospital and help him get the treatment he needs?' I took that on," he recalls. Kapil contacted the chief medical officer and helped the child receive treatment and spectacles. "If you do something with genuine intention, without expecting anything in return, it gives you a different kind of satisfaction," he says. Kapil and his friends founded Parivartan in October 2016 and registered it in July 2017. Their early work included riverbank awareness, air pollution and women's empowerment through street plays and role plays. "There was no fixed project or particular cause in mind," he says. "We felt that we wanted to do something about social issues. So, we would meet, discuss what we could do, make a plan, and then take it to the ground." "It was largely a process of trial and error," he says. Some members left as they completed engineering or MBA courses and chose other careers. Kapil continued with a smaller team, gradually recognising that he wanted to work in the social sector. Why did the waste keep coming back? In November 2016, Kapil sat beside the Ramganga during a riverside festival, watching plastic bags, flowers, clothes and household waste enter the water. He began talking to visitors about what they were discarding. "We have a living river in our city. It was once the lifeline of the communities living along its banks. But today, industrial waste, sewage and all kinds of solid waste are being dumped into it," he recalls. The conversations showed him that people needed practical alternatives. The team explained how flowers and other organic offerings could be composted in a designated pit, while plastic and other non-biodegradable waste could go to municipal collection. Visitors responded positively. The team explained how flowers and other organic offerings could be composted in a designated pit. On Earth Day, 22 April 2018, the team formally launched the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign. Three months of Sunday clean-ups at a ghat (riverside steps) were followed by a wall mural and an 11,000-signature campaign. They carried the signatures on a cycle yatra (journey) from Moradabad to Varanasi, passing through Rampur, Bareilly, Shahjahanpur, Sitapur, Lucknow, Raebareli and Prayagraj. Yet the work at the riverbank exposed a problem. "What we were doing earlier wasn't sustainable," he says. "We would clean the ghat for three months, but once we stopped, it would eventually return to the same condition." Between 2018 and 2020, the team stayed involved through monthly engagement, festival clean-ups and awareness activities, without a fixed weekly schedule. COVID-19 then interrupted public activities. Parivartan worked with the district administration and volunteers to provide essential supplies to marginalised communities. Kapil also remembers seeing distant hills from Moradabad's rooftops during the lockdown, when the air was clearer. The experience reinforced his interest in sustained environmental work. "It made us realise that environmental work cannot be a one-time effort. The real difference comes when you keep showing up and continue the work," he says. This time, there would be no end date On World Environment Day, 5 June 2021, the team began a new phase at Lalbagh Ghat. Household waste and discarded offerings littered the bank, with few awareness messages or conversations about pollution. Kapil wanted the clean-ups to become a regular commitment. "We told our teammates and volunteers that this was not something we would do for a few weeks or months. We were in it for the long run, for the Ram Ganga," he says. In summer, volunteers generally work from around 6.30 am to 9 am; in winter, they start closer to 7.30 am. "We keep track of the numbers, document our progress and assess the impact to understand how the campaign is making a difference," he says. He says Sunday engagement has continued since then, with awareness activities replacing physical clean-ups when flooding or excessive rain makes the riverbank unsafe. In summer, volunteers generally work from around 6.30 am to 9 am; in winter, they start closer to 7.30 am. Kapil or a teammate briefs them before they begin. "All the volunteers come together with their gloves and other equipment," he explains. "I brief them on what needs to be done and what kind of waste we need to collect . If I'm not there, my teammates take over and guide everyone through the work." The focus is on plastic and other non-biodegradable waste. Depending on weather, season and footfall, a Sunday clean-up can yield around 300 to 700 kg, he says. The team segregates waste wherever possible. Flowers and organic offerings go into the composting pit. Recovered idols are kept out of the river. Other inorganic waste is handed to the municipal corporation for treatment and disposal, with recyclable material sent for recovery where possible. Alongside collection, volunteers speak to visitors about the available disposal facilities and ways to reduce waste. Those conversations have become central to keeping the bank clean. Changing a familiar habit takes patience "Behavioural change is a very tough thing," Kapil says. During the Navratri mela (fair), he estimates that 15,000 to 20,000 people visit the nearby temple each day, increasing the pressure on the riverbank. Some visitors told volunteers they were following practices passed down through their families. The team explained how they could continue observing their customs while using the waste facilities. Kapil says most visitors now use the designated pit or other disposal facilities. Announcements from the temple also encourage people to keep waste and offerings away from the bank, reinforcing the volunteers' message. On Earth Day, 22 April 2018, the team formally launched the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign. Mansi Mehrotra, 25, has been associated with Parivartan since December 2017. She joined after seeing waste around the river and recalls how much patience one conversation required. "Raising awareness was only the first step. We realised that real change would come only when we took action ourselves," she says. During a clean-up, she met a man planning to immerse plaster of Paris idols. He initially resisted her explanation of their environmental impact. The team continued talking to him, and eventually he took the idols back. "Sometimes, creating change requires patience, meaningful conversations and helping people understand why it matters," she says. Vikrant, 38, a waste collection vehicle driver with Nagar Nigam Moradabad, regularly visits the ghat and has witnessed the volunteers' work. "We have seen the change almost every week," he says. "The difference is clearly visible to the naked eye." "I have watched these youngsters working every Sunday for years, and their consistency has influenced me as well," he says. Giving people a reason to return The campaign's participants include students, professionals, residents, National Cadet Corps (NCC) and National Service Scheme (NSS) volunteers, and people from social organisations and community groups. Parivartan has more than 3,000 registered volunteers, while six full-time staff members work specifically on the Ramganga campaign. Kapil says staff join Sunday clean-ups as volunteers too. "Every Sunday we reach there because we consider it our social responsibility," he explains. The team also wants people to enjoy their time by the river. After a week in offices or colleges, volunteers can spend time outdoors, talk to vendors, and watch people farming and gardening nearby. There are pets playing, picnics, river festivals and stand-up sessions after clean-ups. "When people get the chance to come to the riverbank, take part in activities and observe the community around them, they really enjoy the experience," he says. Clean-ups also mark occasions such as Independence Day , Republic Day and Gandhi Jayanti. Over the years, participants have planted hundreds of trees, beautified public spaces and created awareness murals. The campaign received India Book of Records recognition for the "Longest Cleanliness Drive on a Riverbank Organised by an NGO". Kapil also sees its influence in volunteers' choices elsewhere. "I don't think any of these volunteers would litter on a riverbank, whether it is the Ram Ganga or any other river. Some of our volunteers are also involved in beach clean-ups in Mumbai, while others are part of clean-up efforts in Dehradun," he says. Old newspapers help pay for the next clean-up Keeping the work going requires funds as well as time. Through its SEHYOG initiative, Parivartan collects old newspapers, books, plastics and other recyclable material from households and well-wishers in door-to-door drives. The material is sold to authorised scrap dealers, and the proceeds help fund the organisation's social and environmental initiatives, including the Ramganga campaign. Individual donors and well-wishers contribute towards cleaning materials, awareness activities and other expenses. Local support also helps volunteers organise clean-ups when the core team cannot attend. "Even if no one from our team is able to come, you can still collect the tools and carry out the clean-up yourselves," Kapil tells them. Between 2018 and 2020, the team stayed involved through monthly engagement, festival clean-ups and awareness activities. Taking the river's problems to the authorities Kapil knows that removing solid waste addresses only part of the river's pollution. Untreated sewage needs action beyond the Sunday clean-ups. The team has submitted a 10-point action agenda and its 200-week campaign booklet to the National Mission for Clean Ganga and the State Mission for Clean Ganga. Kapil wants sewage treatment plants to function efficiently so wastewater from city drains is treated before entering the river. "The Ram Ganga is the tributary of the Ganga, and cleaning the Ganga is not possible without cleaning the Ram Ganga," he says. His ambition is a model ghat where people can visit, observe their customs and spend time by the water while keeping the surroundings clean. He says Sunday engagement has continued since then, with awareness activities replacing physical clean-ups when flooding or excessive rain makes the riverbank unsafe. "For us, the greatest achievement has never been the kilograms of waste removed from the Ramganga," he says. "It has been the change in people's behaviour." That change already has a place in Chotu's home, where the cleaning tools remain ready for whoever comes to collect them next Sunday. All pictures courtesy Parivartan "The Change".

items.descriptionOriginal: In the search for a sustainable alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries, researchers often look to materials found readily in nature . And in the latest such advance, researchers in Spain have made a rechargeable battery that uses vitamin B12 as a catalyst. Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that the body needs for making red blood cells and maintaining the nervous system. The human body doesn’t naturally produce vitamin B12, and it is usually obtained from animal products such as fish, meat, and dairy. The food and drug industry cultivate bacteria that produce vitamin B12 for supplements and additives. The team from the University of Cordoba decided to put the vitamin to use in zinc-air batteries. Metal-air batteries are more sustainable than lithium-ion batteries, which rely on expensive critical minerals that are mined with an environmental and ethical cost. Metal–air batteries consist of a negative electrode made of pure metal such as lithium, magnesium, aluminum, or zinc. The positive electrode has a porous structure that lets in oxygen from the air, and a catalyst at the electrode triggers electrochemical reactions with the oxygen. “Precisely because it uses atmospheric oxygen, one of the battery’s active materials is not located inside the battery itself, thus significantly reducing its weight,” the researchers write in a paper published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A . So metal–air batteries can pack much more energy by weight than conventional lithium-ion batteries. This makes them promising for applications where light weight is crucial, such as drones or medical devices. Indeed, small zinc-air batteries, the most practical among the different types of metal–air batteries, are used widely for hearing aids. turn your house into a battery The Cordoba team wanted to make a rechargeable battery using a biomolecule. They have previously made batteries with the protein hemoglobin and the enzyme catalase, which contain iron. This time they chose vitamin B12, also called cobalamin. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its core, which would be essential for electrochemical reactions. Vitamin B12 is a highly soluble vitamin. To make it stable inside a battery that operates with water-based electrolytes, the team fixed it to the surface of carbon nanotubes, which are microscopic tubes made of carbon atoms. Then the researchers incorporated the nanotubes into the air electrode of alkaline zinc-air batteries. The electrodes reached a specific capacity of 199.4 mAh of energy per gram, giving rechargeable batteries with high performance. And the electrodes worked in a cyclic fashion, allowing for a battery that could be recharged for up to 250 cycles. The performance is far from what is needed for practical applications right now, but the work highlights biomolecular platforms as “a high-performance and sustainable frontier for next-generation rechargeable batteries,” writes the team. items.title: Πώς το Navi Mumbai τελείωσε την 8χρονη βασιλεία της καθαριότητας του Indore και τι μπορεί να μάθει η Βομβάη
items.titleOriginal: How Navi Mumbai Ended Indore’s 8-Year Cleanliness Reign and What Mumbai Can Learn
items.description: Για οκτώ συναπτά έτη, η Indore κατείχε την πρώτη θέση στην ετήσια κατάταξη καθαριότητας της Ινδίας. Η Navi Mumbai τερμάτισε πρώτη στο Super Swachh League μεταξύ 4,7…
items.descriptionOriginal: For eight consecutive years, Indore held the top spot in India's annual cleanliness rankings. On 11 November 2026, that run ended in New Delhi, where President Droupadi Murmu presented Navi Mumbai's Mayor, Sujata Patil, with the cleanest city award at the 10th Swachh Survekshan Awards. Navi Mumbai finished first in the Super Swachh League among 4,751 cities, ahead of Surat and Vijayawada. The result has revived a comparison with Mumbai, the city next door, and a common misconception that needs clearing up. A twin city, but not a suburb Many people assume Navi Mumbai is simply part of Mumbai, which is not the case. It was planned as a satellite city across Thane Creek after Greater Mumbai's population doubled from three million to nearly six million between 1951 and 1971, and the City and Industrial Development Corporation (CIDCO) was formed in 1971 to build it on marshland and former village land. From GPS-tracked garbage trucks to citizen-led cleanliness drives, Navi Mumbai's winning formula goes beyond keeping its streets spotless. Photograph: ( Free Press Journal ) The Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation (NMMC) began functioning only in 1992, governs the nodes from Airoli to Belapur, and is headed by its own mayor and municipal commissioner, while Mumbai is run by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC). Navi Mumbai grew out of Mumbai's need for space but was never carved out of the older city, so the award belongs to the NMMC alone, and its significance is clearest against the city it displaced. What Indore got right first To see what Navi Mumbai had to beat, start with Indore's long reign, which rested on unglamorous sequencing . Its corporation began a door-to-door collection pilot in two of 85 wards in January 2016 and reached 100% coverage by the end of that year, according to a Global Methane Initiative case study. Households now separate waste into six streams, a GPS-tracked fleet reports to a central command centre, and fines for non-segregation and littering back the system, as the city's former collector has written. Clean streets need more than sanitation workers. Navi Mumbai's model brings together technology, waste segregation and citizen participation to keep the city clean. Photograph: ( India Today ) Its bio-CNG plant also turns wet waste into fuel for city buses. Indore remains a strong performer, finishing second in the new Mentor City category behind Ahmedabad, so overtaking it required more than a copy of its model. How Navi Mumbai pulled ahead Navi Mumbai, which placed third behind Indore and Surat in the previous edition, built comparable discipline and added layers of its own. Its Integrated Command and Control Centre tracks garbage vehicles by GPS, and residents file complaints and follow their resolution through the MyNMMC app and a Citizen Grievance Portal. The city has held the Seven-Star Garbage-Free City rating and Water Plus certification, treats 100% of its sewage, and has curbed plastic while drawing students and youth into cleanliness drives. Waste and Recycling magazine describes its Textile Recovery Facility at Belapur, built with the Union Ministry of Textiles' Textile Committee, as the country's first municipal facility of its kind, though housing societies were slow to adopt the bins and segregation at source remains inconsistent. Planned as a satellite city to ease Mumbai's growing population, Navi Mumbai has now outshone its older neighbour in urban cleanliness. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) Commissioner Dr Kailas Shinde credits technology and public participation, and the NMMC dates the climb to three to four years of sustained effort under the motto Nischay Kela, Number Pahila, meaning determined to be number one. The same measures tell a different story in Mumbai. Where Mumbai stands In the 2024-25 survey, Greater Mumbai was listed eighth among the 10 lowest-scoring cities with populations above 10 lakh, according to Deccan Herald. The BMC handles more than 6,500 tonnes of waste a day, around 5,900 tonnes of it going to the Kanjurmarg landfill, and Free Press Journal reports that limited public participation and the lack of 100% segregation have slowed its goal of a zero-garbage city by 2030. Air quality adds to the strain. Newslaundry counted only seven days of 'good' air across the five winters from 2021 to 2026, and the BMC identifies construction dust as a major contributor, with around 3,200 active construction sites. While Mumbai struggles with mounting waste and construction dust, its neighbour Navi Mumbai offers a blueprint for cleaner, more sustainable urban living. Photograph: (TNIE) The BMC counts 231 good or satisfactory air days up to 22 October 2026, against 218 in 2025, so the trend is mixed. Each of these problems has a counterpart in Navi Mumbai's methods. What Mumbai can borrow Three practices stand out, and each answers a gap described above. The first is enforced source segregation, since the BMC has yet to reach 100% segregation. Indore piloted collection ward by ward and backed it with fines, and the Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 now require four-way segregation nationwide, with bulk waste generators processing waste on site. The second is live monitoring, which matters at the scale of the BMC's 6,500 tonnes a day, and both Indore and Navi Mumbai track collection vehicles from command centres. The third is recycled water for dust. The NMMC has made tertiary treated water mandatory at construction sites and uses it in dust-suppression vehicles and road washing, a practical answer to the dust that the BMC names as a major contributor to pollution. Mumbai's scale will make the task harder, and experts quoted by Newstrack call the ranking only a first step, with year-round upkeep the real test. The NMMC is already preparing a Sugandhi Shahar Abhiyan, or Fragrant City Campaign, to build on the win. Sources ' Swachh Sarvekshan Awards: Navi Mumbai Grabs Top Spot In Super Swachh League, Surat Ranked Second ': by ETV Bharat English Team for ETV Bharat, Published on 11 November, 2026 ' Navi Mumbai Ranks India's Cleanest City Among 4,751 Urban Centres In Swachh Survekshan 2025-26 ': by Raina Assainar for Free Press Journal, Published on 11 November, 2026 ' How India's Cleanest City Reduces Methane Emissions from Municipal Solid Waste ': by Global Methane Initiative for Global Methane Initiative ' FPJ News Positive: BMC's 28,000 Sanitation Workers Battle 6,500 MT Daily Waste Amid Rising Challenges Of Construction Debris And Illegal Dumping ': by author not credited for Free Press Journal, date not shown (about October 2025) ' 7 'good' air days in 5 years: How coastal Mumbai normalised chronic pollution ': by author not credited for Newslaundry, Published on 10 March, 2026
