items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe Reading Time: 3 minutes Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has helped saiga antelope rebound from about 20,000 to 4.6 million. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has produced one of the largest wildlife recoveries on record. Saiga antelope numbers have climbed from roughly 20,000 in the early 2000s to about 4.6 million in 2026. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has led this work since 2006. Altyn Dala means “golden steppe” in Kazakh. The initiative has helped protect 5 million hectares of grassland, an area larger than Denmark. It is also bringing back wild asses and wild horses that vanished from the region long ago. The saiga is a small antelope with a large, flexible nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Its herds migrate hundreds of miles across the steppe, a vast, dry grassland with few trees. By the early 2000s, those herds had nearly disappeared. After the Soviet Union collapsed, poaching surged across Central Asia. Hunters killed saigas for meat and for male horns, which sold for traditional medicine in Asia. Within about a decade, the population crashed by more than 95%. Five partners joined forces in 2006 to reverse that decline. Kazakhstan’s Committee for Forestry and Wildlife works with the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. Fauna & Flora, the Frankfurt Zoological Society, and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds bring international support. Their first priority was stopping the killing. Ranger teams and aerial patrols now cover the saiga’s range. Sniffer dogs and customs training help catch horn smugglers at the border. Next, the partners needed to know where the herds went. Since 2009, researchers have fitted saigas with satellite tags to map their migrations. That data shows which areas need protection and when. New reserves followed the herds. The most recent, Bokey Orda-Ashiozek in western Kazakhstan, covers about 657,000 hectares. Wildlife corridors also link reserves through private land, under joint plans with landowners. The strategy faced its hardest test in 2015. During the spring calving season, more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks, over 60% of the global population. A 2018 study in Science Advances linked the deaths to a bacterium that turned deadly in hot, humid weather. Because poaching was under control, the surviving herds could rebuild. Aerial surveys each spring tracked the comeback. The 2024 count found about 2.8 million saigas, and the 2026 count reached roughly 4.6 million. That is about 230 times the low point. In December 2023, the IUCN Red List moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. The Kazakh association’s director, Vera Voronova, called it one of the most successful land mammal recoveries ever recorded. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe means rebuilding the full community of grazing animals, not just one species. Kulan, a wild ass native to Central Asia, disappeared from the Torgai steppe more than 100 years ago. Scientists consider them a keystone species, since their grazing and movement help shape the grassland. Reintroductions began in 2017, and partners aim to establish about 100 kulan in the region. A recent group traveled 2,139 kilometers by road from Altyn-Emel National Park. After a year in an acclimatization pen, the animals went free in August 2025. Przewalski’s horses are following the same path. Considered the last truly wild horse species, they vanished from the wild by 1969 and survived only in zoos. In Kazakhstan, they had been gone for about 200 years. Przewalski’s horses returning to the wild are part of restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe after about 200 years. Photo by Wijs (Wise) on Pexels. The first seven horses arrived at the Altyn Dala reserve in 2024. More followed in 2025 from Prague Zoo and Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park. In May 2026, five of them left their pens and began roaming free. Officials plan to bring 40 to 45 horses by 2029, enough to sustain the herd. A stallion named Galvan wears a GPS collar so rangers can follow his movements. Local support makes these gains last. The initiative runs education programs in rural schools and has published children’s books about steppe wildlife in Kazakh. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe depends on the next generation valuing these animals. Recovery has also created new tensions. Farmers in several regions report that saigas damage crops and compete with livestock for pasture. Authorities are now studying how to manage herd sizes without undoing two decades of conservation. Roads, railways, and fences still break up migration routes. Wildfires and farm expansion put pressure on ground-nesting birds. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe will require balancing people and wildlife for years to come. Twenty years ago, the saiga seemed headed for extinction. Today, millions roam the plains, joined by wild asses and horses returning after a century or more. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe shows what patient, well-coordinated protection can achieve. The post Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αντί να τα εγκαταλείψει όλα, δημοσίευσε μια ανώνυμη πρόσκληση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης και 11 γυναίκες από τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, τον Καναδά και την Ουαλία είπαν ναι - σε έναν ξένο, μια χώρα, μια…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.

items.title: Οι δερματολόγοι σχολιάζουν την τάση TikTok να τρώτε το δέρμα σας
items.titleOriginal: Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Εάν η σελίδα σας For You ήταν γεμάτη από άτομα που ακυρώνουν ραντεβού για μπότοξ επειδή άρχισαν να τρώνε περισσότερο σολομό, έχετε βρει την τάση "eat your skincare". Η υπόθεση είναι ότι η σωστή διατροφή μπορεί να κάνει αυτό που υπόσχεται ένα ντουλάπι φαρμάκων γεμάτο ορούς. Είναι, ειλικρινά, ελκυστικό… αλλά είναι επίσης μόνο εν μέρει tr…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If your For You Page has been full of people canceling Botox appointments because they started eating more salmon, you’ve found the “eat your skincare” trend. The premise is that the right diet can do what a medicine cabinet full of serums promises. It is, honestly, an appealing one… but it’s also only partly true. The route food takes to your skin When you eat, nutrients get absorbed in the GI tract and travel through the bloodstream to wherever your body decides to send them. There’s no targeting involved, so your skin gets what’s available once everything else takes its share. Topical skincare works on a different logic entirely, putting concentrated ingredients directly on one spot without the detour. “Wrinkles and collagen loss are multifactorial,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets , Director of Cosmetic Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “No single food or supplement is going to make a huge difference if the rest of your diet is poor, you are unhealthy or dealing with inflammation, excessive sun exposure or you don’t have a good skincare regimen.” Food can correct deficiencies that slow things down. Vitamin C and amino acids matter for collagen formation; fatty acids support the skin barrier. But more doesn’t mean more. “I think of it as filling the tank,” Dr. Kobets says. “You need the nutrients and building blocks, but overfilling it doesn’t make the collagen-making machinery work faster.” Too much vitamin C, she notes, can cause GI problems and, in some people, raise the risk of kidney stones. Can food protect you from the sun? Some of the content goes further: eat your sunscreen . That sounds ridiculous, but there’s real science underneath it. “There is interesting evidence around oral photoprotection ,” Dr. Kobets says. “Certain carotenoids, polyphenols and Polypodium leucotomos extract have been studied for increasing the skin’s resistance to UV-induced damage.” That’s not a reason to put the SPF away, though. “I sometimes think of these as an extra layer of defense, but definitely not an oral sunscreen,” she says. “No amount of blueberries, green tea or antioxidant supplements is going to replace properly applied and reapplied sunscreen, protective clothing and smart sun behavior.” What to eat for skin health If you want your diet to pull some weight here, the list is manageable. Dr. Sapna Palep , a dermatologist at Journelle Skin, recommends eggs, avocado, flaxseeds, walnuts, salmon, and dark chocolate, which between them cover protein, healthy fats, omega-3 fatty acids , and antioxidants. “Nutrition can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, the microbiome and skin-barrier function,” says Dr. Kobets. “What is good for your overall metabolic health tends to be good for your skin as well.” That’s the version of this trend that holds up: eating well really does support your skin, and the foods involved are things most of us would benefit from eating more of anyway. What food can’t do is replace sunscreen or stand in for a routine that’s doing something. Think of it as filling a role, not playing every position. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Real-Life "Babe": Νεογέννητο γουρουνάκι που διασώθηκε από την άκρη του δρόμου είναι τώρα ένας αγαπημένος κάτοικος στο καταφύγιο ζώων φάρμας
items.titleOriginal: Real-Life “Babe”: Newborn Piglet Rescued From Roadside Is Now a Beloved Resident at Farm Animal Sanctuary
items.description: Ένα γουρουνάκι που σώθηκε από μια δυνητικά πολύ κακή μοίρα ζει τώρα την ιστορία του Μπέιμπ, αφού το πήρε μέσα από μια συμπονετική προγιαγιά που έχει ένα καταφύγιο ζώων στην Αγγλία. Η συνταξιούχος κτηνιατρική νοσοκόμα Carole Webb έσωσε τον μικροσκοπικό άνθρωπο, που ονομάστηκε Tom, αφού τον ανακάλυψαν στην άκρη του δρόμου τον Μάρτιο σε ηλικία μόλις 1 ημέρας. Είναι ασαφές…
items.descriptionOriginal: A piglet saved from a potentially much unkinder fate is now living out the story of Babe after being taken in by a compassionate great-grandmother who owns an animal sanctuary in England. Retired veterinary nurse Carole Webb rescued the tiny fellow, dubbed Tom, after he was discovered on the side of the road in March at just 1 day old. It’s unclear how he came to be there, but Webb theorized that a sow may have given birth while being transported, and the piglet fell from the trailer. The person who found him kept him safe overnight before handing him over to her. FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Tom, who was about the size of a kitten at the time, was hand-reared indoors with hot water bottles and heat pads. Six months later, he’s grown into a pampered pig roaming a three-acre field at the Farm Animal Rescue Sanctuary in Stratford-upon-Avon. “Tom is really just like a real-life Babe,” Webb, 82, told SWNS, adding: “He’s really friendly with the chickens, he’s got a lot of chicken and cat friends — really anything that goes in to see him is his friend.” She said he acts more like a pet dog now than a typical pig, following the farm’s humans around and even coming when he’s called by name. He also has his own stuffed animals, loves to play, and enjoys his treats. “He plays around you and loves being near you. He’s got a big fluffy toy pig, and what he likes to do is lay over it,” she noted. “He loves his belly rubs, too — he’s just the friendliest little pig you could meet.” FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Named after Lord of the Rings character Tom Bombadil , Tom now weighs around 330-450 pounds, a big jump from the tiny piglet that could once fit in the palm of Webb’s hand. “He’s a bit boisterous so we don’t mix him with the sheep, but he’s got the run of one of the field,” said Webb. She noted that the sanctuary is home to about 350 animals, including sheep, cats, chickens, and one other pig. “We also feed the pigeons that are free-flying, and we’ve got an aviary that we put them in until they’re well,” she added. “We’ve got quite a collection.” The sanctuary is currently raising money to buy new land so it can continue caring for its animals. Donate here. This article was originally written by Adam Dutton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. items.title: Τέσσερις άνδρες, τέσσερις χώρες, ένας κανόνας
items.titleOriginal: Four Men, Four Countries, One Rule
items.description: Σε μια κηδεία ενός ανθρώπου που δεν είπε ποτέ σε κανέναν ότι ήταν δυστυχισμένος, οι φίλοι που επέζησαν κάθισαν γύρω από ένα τραπέζι και μίλησαν για παιχνίδια στον υπολογιστή. Αυτή η λεπτομέρεια -- ακριβής και επώδυνη -- είναι το σημείο όπου ξεκινά αυτό το δοκίμιο και θέτει όλα όσα ακολουθούν. Ο συγγραφέας Rajeev Balasubramanyam παρακολούθησε τη θλίψη στο δωμάτιο να θάβεται υπό απόσπαση της προσοχής και αποφάσισε κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: At a funeral for a man who never told anyone he was unhappy, the surviving friends sat around a table and talked about computer games. That detail -- precise and painful -- is where this essay begins, and it sets up everything that follows. Writer Rajeev Balasubramanyam watched the grief in the room get buried under distraction and decided something had to change. He called three old friends scattered across Vancouver, London, Brussels, and Berlin, and he proposed the thing none of them had ever done: a men's circle. The rules were simple -- take turns speaking while others listen and no advice-giving. That last rule proved harder than it sounds; as he notes, dispensing solutions is simply "the way that we, as men, were used to talking." What emerged instead was something quieter and more rare: the feeling of being held. Over a year of online circles, a father died, a cancer survivor admitted he wasn't as fine as he'd thought, and a man in grief finally had space to feel it.

items.title: 10 παραδόσεις ευεξίας από όλο τον κόσμο για να μπείτε στη ζωή σας
items.titleOriginal: 10 Wellness Traditions From Around the World to Weave Into Your Life
items.description: Η λέξη «ευεξία» μπορεί να δημιουργεί εικόνες από πολυτελείς περιποιήσεις σπα και πολυτελή καταφύγια, αλλά δεν χρειάζεται να κλείσετε μια πολυτελή απόδραση για να αυξήσετε τη ζωτικότητά σας – οι καθημερινές δραστηριότητες και οι μικρές, σκόπιμες συνήθειες μπορούν να είναι εξίσου αναζωογονητικές. Διαφορετικοί πολιτισμοί σε όλο τον κόσμο έχουν αναπτύξει εδώ και καιρό μοναδικές τεχνικές για την προώθηση της υγείας, της ευτυχίας και γενικότερα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The word “wellness” may conjure images of lavish spa treatments and high-end retreats, but you don’t have to book a luxury getaway to increase your vitality — everyday activities and small, intentional habits can be equally restorative. Different cultures around the world have long developed unique techniques to promote health, happiness, and overall well-being, from the Turkish concept of savoring idle pleasure to “forest bathing” in Japan. Join us as we explore 10 wellness traditions you can adopt to infuse more peace and balance into our often-overwhelming world. 1. Schemeren | The Netherlands antolikjan/iStock If you struggle to unwind after a long day, the Dutch concept of “dusking,” or “schemeren,” may be just what you’re looking for. The practice is remarkably effortless: Simply pull up a chair and pause for a while to watch the day turn into night. “Noticing twilight requires a persistent kind of attention. It’s like a shy, rare animal. You have to take your time. Stay focused,” author Marjolijn van Heemstra told the BBC , adding that it’s an important opportunity to reconnect with the world around us. “If you don’t know a tree, even if it’s in front of your house, because you never take the time to look at it, you don’t mind it being cut,” she said. “So, it’s about seeing things and trying to establish a relationship with them and then maybe caring for them.” 2. La Passeggiata | Italy Another evening ritual — la passeggiata — is a bit more active. In Italy, many people take an after-dinner stroll around town, which offers a way to connect with neighbors, reduce stress, and improve digestion, per the BBC . Although walking is widely recommended as an accessible and effective exercise , la passeggiata is more about relaxation and social bonds than fitness. 3. Hygge | Denmark Liudmila Chernetska/iStock Scandinavian winters tend to be long and dark, but the Danish tradition of hygge can make the season more enjoyable. Stemming from an Old Norse word meaning “protected from the outside world,” hygge centers on creating a cozy, comfortable environment, with an emphasis on self-care, relaxation, and spending time with loved ones. While it’s often associated with tangible things like warm drinks and soft blankets, it’s also a mindset focused on making small moments feel more meaningful. 4. Ubuntu | Southern Africa In certain sub-Saharan African cultures, including the Zulu and Xhosa, the philosophy and practice of ubuntu emphasize the importance of community and interconnectedness. Although it goes by many different names, ubuntu is apparent throughout societies across the continent, according to The Open University . At its core, it emphasizes the role individuals play in contributing to the greater good through intentional connection, mutual support, and a shared commitment to equality, equity, and fairness. In daily life, this can look like sharing resources and checking in on neighbors. As a whole, it’s about recognizing the humanity in everyone you meet. And the benefits may extend beyond your community: Research suggests that being kind to others can help your own well-being, too. 5. Sobremesa | Spain and Latin America JulieanneBirch/iStock Another custom grounded in community is “sobremesa,” which means “upon the table.” Popular in Spain and throughout Latin America, the centuries-old way of life involves lingering after a meal to relax, savor the moment, and chat — sometimes for hours. “It’s about an interchange of experiences, knowledge, and laughs. It encourages you to be present, not worrying about your troubles, and appreciate the simple moments in life,” Mexico City restaurateur Lorea Olavarri told Food & Wine . 6. Keyif | Turkey Turkey is famous for its hammam spas, but one of its perhaps lesser-known wellness traditions can be embraced anywhere. Keyif, “an ancient art of meaningful idleness,” is a state of mind focused on finding quiet joy in simple pleasures, per Eastern Turkey Tours . Unlike simply unwinding, keyif involves being fully present and savoring the more subdued moments, from sipping your first cup of coffee in the morning while watching the sun rise to gazing out the window and listening to the birds. 7. Dadirri | Australia Thurtell/iStock In Australia’s First Nations communities, the art of deep, intentional listening — often called dadirri — is an integral part of cultural preservation, community cohesion, and individual well-being. The ancient practice encourages people to connect with one another and the natural world, according to Aboriginal learning platform Creative Spirits . But it also extends beyond that to encompass self-reflection, contemplation, and an awareness of your origins, purpose, and place in the world. “It does wonders for a person to just be still and listen to someone else talk about their life and how they probably came through things,” late Aboriginal singer-songwriter Archie Roach once said about the importance of mindful listening, per the platform, adding: “You never know what you’ll learn.” 8. Shinrin-Yoku | Japan Ample research points to the mental and physical benefits of spending time in nature, and the Japanese tradition of shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, can help you reap them. Despite the name, there are no bathtubs involved, and even the forest is optional. All it takes is spending some time in a green space and using your senses to take it all in, whether at a botanical garden, city park, or lush woodland. Touch the soft moss, breathe in the fresh air, and listen to the birds as you gaze at the trees. “Forest therapy [can help us] see the truth that we are interconnected and interdependent. It offers us intentional time to be with ourselves, each other, and the natural world,” Regan Stacey, founder of The Forest Therapy School , told Vogue . 9. Friluftsliv | Norway Glenn Pettersen/iStock Meaning “open-air living,” this philosophy focuses on connecting with nature year-round, regardless of the weather. Popularized in the 1850s by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, friluftsliv remains a cultural mainstay throughout Scandinavia, according to the BBC . In fact, many employers in the region build outdoor recreation time into the workday. Although a Monday morning hike may not be realistic for everyone, we can all embrace friluftsliv by setting aside time to venture outside as often as we can. 10. Rhythmic Movement and Dance | Various African Cultures While not a singular tradition, dance is central to numerous cultures across the African continent and its diasporas . Although often ritualistic or ceremonial, moving one’s body rhythmically to music is also an integral part of everyday life that can foster both community and individual well-being. “Dancing is a full-body workout that benefits both the mind and body,” Liza Osagie-Clouard, orthopedic surgeon and founder of Solice Health in London, England, told British Vogue . “It improves cardiovascular health, increases flexibility, strengthens muscles, and enhances coordination,” she added. Moreover, listening to music — including the rhythmic drumming that often accompanies traditional dances — can stimulate the release of chemicals like dopamine and serotonin in the brain, helping to alleviate anxiety, enhance mood, and facilitate emotional release.
